articles.title: Exterminauts Wants You to Live a 9-to-5 Life That Bites Back | IGN Preview
articles.summary: Exterminauts is chaotic. Whether you’re blowing your friends up by accident or getting knocked off of a tall structure you’re trying to fix or just reacting to stuff going wrong on the fly, you’re always making decisions and dealing with something beyond your control, and according to the developers, that’s intentional. I felt it during my demo, and it’s one of the aspects of Exterminauts I enjoyed most.
articles.body:
It’s a three-player PvE shooter with a novel premise: you’re an everyman in a sci-fi world.

Jobs that required cooperation were among my favorites during my hands-on session.

Chaos and tension are baked into the gameplay, which added to my enjoyment of it.

Video games generally want you to feel special. We play chosen ones, genetically enhanced soldiers in power armor, superheroes, major and minor deities, legendary swordsmen. We live out lives that are very unlike our own. That’s the fantasy. With Exterminauts, developer Behaviour Interactive wants you to be a working man. Don’t get me wrong, you’ll still be visiting faraway planets and battling some really wild alien beasties. But ultimately, you’re working a 9-to-5. You’re not hunting for glory here. Your job is to get in, do what needs done, and get out. And based on what I played at Gamescom, this could be a job I could grow to love.

That working man mentality undergirds most of what Exterminauts is about. You’re not wearing armor; you’re clad in an orange worksuit you might see at a job site. You’re not going to be able to run off and do everything alone. You’ve gotta stick with your teammates if you want to get the job done, and you’ve got a boss in your ear telling you what you’ll need to take care of next. Oh, and while you may be on a far-off planet full of strange and wondrous flora and fauna, you’re still working for The Man, which is to say, interstellar megacorporations. The more things change, right? Exterminauts has been in development for about five years now, but when I asked members of the team about the game’s identity, they told me that blue collar identity was always part of what they wanted to make.

My demo consisted of a single three-man contract. After we’d chosen our pre-built characters (you’ll have access to customization in the full game, including weapon mods and passive abilities), it was time to get to work. Exterminauts has a low-key vibe to it. Yeah, you’re fighting some absolutely otherworldly monsters (I really liked what looked like air jellyfish, and another bug-like creature) with giant pincers, but everything is very bright, vivid, and colorful. This looks like an alien world full of alien creatures that can fly when you least expect it, burrow underground, and genuinely feel, well, alien – something that’s often hard for games to pull off.

When I asked about it, Creative Director Vincent Regimbald told me nailing that was a lot of work. “I think one of the things that we went for initially was just to try to look at shapes that were really interesting. One of the enemies that you did not see is the wrecking slug. We thought of a Kinder surprise or an egg of sorts. Basically it just rolls around like a big boulder and every now and then it just opens up and there's almost like a yoke inside. It's really gross and that's the weak spot that you shoot at and then it closes back up and starts rolling again. So it's that nice contrast between something that looks incredibly tough and hard and threatening as it's just coming at you, but then on the inside just kind of soft and mushy and really weak. So we always think about our enemies in that way to try to go against expectations a little bit and just try to surprise the audience.”

Thankfully, we were more than equipped for the job. My character occupied more of a support role in my play session. My machine gun was great for smaller fauna, but I also had a deployable turret. My favorite, though, was my rocket launcher, which exploded with cacophonous booms and wiped out anything unlucky enough to be near the blast radius. Extrerminauts also does a neat thing where you can use your backpack to overcharge your heavy weapons, making them even stronger. When something absolutely, positively has to die, accept no substitutes.

But despite its name, Exterminauts isn’t just about blasting away at whatever we found planetside. You also have to do your job. That means traipsing up (or ziplining between) massive structures and doing things like turning valves, fixing electrical shorts, welding metal, or whatever else. One of my favorite sections had me playing what was essentially the pipe connecting minigame from Bioshock while my turret (and my squadmates) held off some local wildlife that really didn’t want us around.

But some problems will require multiple Exterminauts to fix, so you’ll have to coordinate, which was one of my favorite things about my time with it. Even something as simple as turning a pair of valves at the same time can be challenging when you only have one person left to defend the rest of the team. I also dug that you could fasttrack some of these fixes if you were willing to give something up. Sure, I could play the minigame to get that terminal back online, but I could also just juice it with my backpack if I had the power to spare.

“We looked at a lot of the typical things that a blue-collar worker might do on a work site,” Regimbald told me when I asked about how they approached designing the jobs players would need to do. “So we only saw a portion here, but there is welding, there are terminals that are shut down that need to be rebooted. There's electrical systems that are offline that need to be rebooted. So it's a lot of interaction points.”

I also liked how Exterminauts makes you traverse its world. Things aren’t flat; the buildings you’ll climb and the environments you’ll navigate are replete with gorges and cliffs you’ll need ziplines to navigate. Or you could, like me, just slide off the smaller ones and hope you could time a roll as you were about to land to mitigate the fall damage. Half the time, the first part of any job was asking, “Okay, how do we get up there?”

Once we’d finished rebooting all the terminals, fixing welds, dropping in new pipe, and clearing off weird goop that had accumulated on the machines we needed to maintain, it was time to go home. No job is done until you clock out, after all – and you do literally clock in and out in Exterminauts. Once we called in a dropship to take us home, it was time to hold out until it arrived. My turret put in work, but at this point I figured I’d juice up my rocket launcher and play around with it a bit. It worked great, but I also accidentally killed a couple of my teammates – and if you run out of lives, it’s contract failed. Whoops.

And that’s the other thing about Exterminauts, and something that you might not get from watching a trailer: it’s chaotic. Whether you’re blowing your friends up by accident or getting knocked off of a tall structure you’re trying to fix or just reacting to stuff going wrong on the fly, you’re always making decisions and dealing with something beyond your control, and according to the developers, that’s intentional. I felt it during my demo, and it’s one of the aspects of Exterminauts I enjoyed most.

Eventually, our dropship arrived and we made it off-planet and back to base. That was it. Demo over. I was sorry to see us clock out, but I am excited to see what kind of work I can pick up as an Exterminaut in the future. Oh, and those mods sound neat, too, especially the ice one that lets you freeze and shatter enemies. Until then, I’ll be workin’ 9-to-5, trying to make a living. Just like an Exterminaut, but without the aliens and scary falls. But you know what they say: any job you can walk away from is a good one, right?

While you're here, check out these recent previews of other big upcoming games we've checked out recently!

Will Borger is an IGN freelancer. You can find him on Bluesky @edgarallanbro.

articles.title: Warlock: Dungeons & Dragons Doesn't Have Waypoints Because the Devs Want Players to 'Figure Things Out' for Themselves
articles.summary: The developers of Warlock: Dungeons & Dragons have said they avoided putting waypoints into the game because they want players to actually explore.
articles.body:
The developers of Warlock: Dungeons & Dragons have said they avoided putting waypoints into the game because they want players to actually explore.

The open-world single-player action-adventure goes easy on the hand-holding by ditching traditional quest markers that guide players directly from one story section to the next. While it does have a compass on the top of the screen — which you can turn off — the player is left to work out where to go by exploring, talking to NPCs, and thinking about what to do next.

Dominic Guay, General Manager at Invoke Studios, told IGN at gamescom 2026 the decision was all about wanting to encourage exploration. “We wanted them to engage with the world, to figure things out and feel that when they found things, it was based on their actions and not just blindly trusting a waypoint,” he said.

Guay and the rest of the developers at Invoke have experience making open world games that include waypoints, such as Ubisoft’s Watch Dogs series. But this time around, for Warlock, they wanted to do things differently.

“The core team on this game have worked on other open world games before and we've done the, let's say, the heavy-handed guiding approach before,” Guay said. “What ends up happening at some point — and it's normal — a lot of players will just follow blindly the waypoint, and then you lose that agency, you lose that feeling of curiosity because you're like, well, why even bother? And so we didn't want to go there. We wanted the player to explore.”

To that end, Warlock has a Mystery system that are triggered when players take certain actions, typically in a settlement. The idea is players will uncover mysteries by exploring, talking to NPCs, and gathering information, rather than following a quest market to where the Mystery officially kicks off.

“There are multiple entry points,” Guay explained. “They're kind of harder for us to do in that way, but we love that challenge. Not only are there multiple entry points, but depending on how you stumble upon them, it might change how you interact with them, meaning that maybe you could have found actually you can chance upon that Mystery from a completely different place and then it'll lead you toward that settlement, and you'll know before coming in there's something fishy going on here. So then you'll approach that settlement differently than in this case where you learn it from within.

"Some [Mysteries] are a little bit more straightforward, some are a little bit more deep and requires more engagement and exploration, but that's really how they're built."

Video game hand-holding is of course a hot topic right now with the release of PlayStation 5 exclusive Marvel’s Wolverine, which has been criticized for its now infamous “fart gas” — the depiction of Logan’s scent trail as he tracks other characters, chases down enemies, and sniffs out collectibles. Some want to be able to turn it off.

The two games are very different, of course. Warlock is an open-world action adventure with emergent gameplay that comes from its unique magic system, whereas Wolverine is a linear action adventure with combat that takes place in constrained areas. Insomniac’s effort isn’t a quest marker sort of game, but it is interesting to hear Invoke’s philosophy when it comes to player hand-holding, and how it set out to avoid it.

articles.title: Silent Hill: Townfall Could Finally Restore Survival Horror’s Missing Mystery
articles.summary: Recent survival horror games have nailed the format but held players' hands too tightly to allow a genuine sense of terrifying mystery - Silent Hill: Townfall looks set to get the old-school formula just right.
articles.body:
This is an IGN opinion piece from Ceridwen Millington, who has craved horror of all stripes ever since she stumbled through Silent Hill 3’s wretched amusement park. Or perhaps since she first got blown to bony gibs in Half-Life. You might today find her at home in the esoteric weirdness of MyHouse.WAD.

Survival horror is back at the top. Franchises synonymous with the genre, like Silent Hill and Resident Evil, are releasing some of the modern age's most popular titles. Indie games inspired by the genre's past seem to be getting released in droves, too, with the likes of Crow Country and Signalis echoing the classics of the original PlayStation. It's a triumphant change from yesteryear – horror was smothered by action in the mid '00s (just look at the trajectory of EA’s Dead Space trilogy) and in the '10s a promised Silent Hill reboot never made it to shelves. But the enormous, record-breaking success of recent survival horrors might suggest a couple of things: that there was an appetite for genuine survival horror all along, and that we're in the new glory days.

The upcoming Silent Hill: Townfall might perhaps help affirm the latter. But, at least right now, it's impossible to accept that we’ve made it into a new golden age when the genre’s current state still makes you miss the glory days. For all of survival horror’s recent triumphs, the biggest names in the business seem to have forgotten one of the genre’s vital components: mystery. There’s little more terrifying than the unknown, after all.

Some would argue that the genre necessarily changes shape, given its knotty history. A major and commercially successful change can be seen in the introduction of the first-person perspective. Popularised by Amnesia: The Dark Descent and PT , it represented a move away from the genre's conventions – and one that has become central to its second wind. The third-person perspective was bundled up with a range of staples: collecting items, exploring carefully designed environments, moderately challenging puzzling, and switching between combat and evasion. The first person perspective is very much about vulnerability, of forcing terror into your face and giving you little time to react. By reducing your field of vision, it quite literally introduces mystery to the frame – what horrors lie beyond the edges of the screen? This brought Resident Evil back to the fore with its seventh mainline installment, the game’s opening hours putting relentless stalkers right in your face.

But these shocking, very real scares are being eroded over time as studios move towards safe bets. This year’s Resident Evil Requiem exemplifies a deliberate caution around leaning too hard in any direction. There are plenty of fearsome threats in the sequences in which you play as Grace Ashcroft, including a giant pursuing man-baby, an unstoppable girl descending from the ceiling, and numerous unique denizens in the game's starting location. But all of these were revealed in pre-release marketing, stripping Requiem’s most fearsome chapter of its mystery for those who followed the game’s production. Furthermore, Grace’s horror-forward sequences are paired with the chainsaw-slinging, roundhouse-kicking action that makes up Leon’s section of the game, a homage to the very familiar days of Resident Evil 4 and 5 which ultimately devolves into a motorbike chase that feels lifted straight from anime. The game's story becomes subsumed by this balancing act , atmospheric narrative playing second fiddle to people pleasing. The mystery is lost as Requiem plays beloved hit after hit.

A similar phenomenon can be seen in last year’s Silent Hill f , the series' first totally original, full-scale title since 2012. The story promises a different approach than others, taking the horror staple of misogyny and considering it through the lens of '60s Japan. Hinako, the game's protagonist, discovers in true franchise style that her town has become fog-laden and populated by horrible creatures. However, it sacrifices any interesting interaction with its deeper themes by presenting them overtly rather than through unease and mystery. Within moments of the game starting there's a grouchy dad whose attitude sledgehammers home what to expect of the narrative. And as you explore the village, you aren't asked to interpret the elegantly designed creatures, with Hinako finding the time to write succinct descriptions in her journal. Imagine the damage Silent Hill 2 would have wrought on its tale if James had spelled out the psychological meanings of the nurses and Pyramid Head as he encountered them. The best Silent Hill games function like artworks, where characters, motivations, and themes are beguiling hooks. Instead, Silent Hill f has the melodrama and obviousness of a teen drama.

Silent Hill never previously leapt wholesale into battle like Resident Evil did, but fighting has been put at the core of Silent Hill f. It was generally more practical to run, to avoid wasting a perfectly good health item so as not to end up in a bad spot later. Fundamentally, the protagonists were everyday people; not superhuman or even capable fighters. Hinako, despite being a seemingly combat-inexperienced schoolgirl, is able to go toe-to-toe with a range of enemies and dodge, counter, special attack, and survive multiple stabbings. It's rare here to feel like a vulnerable person stuck in nightmares, rather than a gamer looking for the next weapon. Breakable pipes and a rare need to run can't mask that fear feels deliberately softened, the vulnerability of survival horror having been undermined in order to drive sales.

Many of the things that new games are doing have been done before, and done with more faith in their audience. One of Silent Hill f's themes is beautiful horrors. As the world changes we begin to see a twisted splendor, the town consumed with blood-red flowers and pulsing pink flesh. But I couldn't help but notice this had already been done in The Song of Saya , a 2003 visual novel that, through static images and sound, presents a similar - but more transgressive - tale of a viscera-filled, upended world and twisted perceptions of beauty. Silent Hill’s approach just feels like bringing a well-worn trope to life. There’s no surprise in this concoction, given the developers were outspoken on trying to craft a beautiful nightmare.

It’s hard to imagine that notorious The Song of Saya didn’t play a part in Silent Hill f’s creation: the latter's writer, Ryukishi07, has created horror visual novels himself. It's unfortunately the case that a visual novel like that isn't backed by a company with colossal revenue, nor will it likely get widespread recognition of its role in horror. Where recent Silent Hill and Resident Evil prepare us for what to expect in their marketing and sanded-off narratives, The Song of Saya leaves us shocked and unsure what to feel. There’s uncertainty from what to take away from the tale, its loved-up protagonists being not just morally compromised but heinous, if pitiable, criminals.

Many obscure parts of the survival horror’s history have had lasting impact, even if they’re not powered by colossal IPs. Clock Tower 3, Haunting Ground, and Rule of Rose are a particularly notable and similar trio, games that had a mixed reception but are now both extremely rare and - by dedicated fans - extremely venerated. One of the things that is obvious across all three titles is their playfulness and absurdities, even considering their serious themes.

Clock Tower 3 is undoubtedly the most striking example of seemingly contradictory-vibes, thanks to its direction by extreme horror maestro Kinji Fukasaku (best known for the Battle Royale movie). Its heroine, Alyssa, must contend with both the cruelty of serial killers and the threat of a vague “possession” now that she’s turning 15. This doesn’t stop Fukasaki and his then-innovative motion capture turning out camp, eccentric, and unforgettable performances. Meaningful themes aren’t presented sombrely and in a didactic fashion, with messages around misogyny left to the subtext. The experience is all the more worthy of reflection for not being plainly laid out.

Most interesting narratively is Rule of Rose , a deeply obscure title best known for commanding a high price on the second-hand market. This year marks its 20th anniversary, and with those two decades of hindsight it’s never been more clear that the trust it put in its players is exceedingly rare. The story follows a young woman, Jennifer, who finds herself deposited at a creepy orphanage - but little time elapses before it bizarrely becomes an airship. It’s not perfect from a gameplay perspective, with the emphasis on backtracking and item collection occasionally getting excessive. Yet this is a trade-off for a world that you belong in and come to know. Grief and suffering aren’t bludgeoned into you immediately as being the core ideas, but are things which come to suffuse the game through surreal vignettes. And, foundational to the experience, it trusts the players to stick with its ambiguities - Jennifer never scribbling down clear analysis in her journal.

Rule of Rose is particularly beloved by devotees of the era because of how it avoids clear-cut answers. It’s more than a female-led twist on Lord of the Flies with its non-linear, dreamlike tale, with a few scenarios playable in any chosen order. The devious nature of this fairy tale is best represented by one of the most unsettling bosses; seemingly doted upon by the orphanage’s lead staff member, she turns from a bedbound child into a “mermaid princess.” What this means is a clawing, vomiting, half-limbless figure swinging from the ceiling of her mortuary-like room. There’s much speculation online as to what’s actually happening here. Abuse? Suicide? The simple powerlessness of childhood? Players are willing to overlook the questionable gameplay; the extensive Wiki suggests a thirst to dig deeply into ideas instead.

There are recent games that have tried to ape the triumphs of the genre’s earlier entries, but most of them seem to be for a hardcore audience looking for raw challenge over genuine horror. It’s a shame, for instance, to pick up an atmosphere-drenched title that doesn’t over-explain its narrative and systems, only to be hampered by limited saves and hard-to-avoid deaths. Difficulty-focused titles like Remothered: Tormented Fathers should exist, but the experience of playing them is almost like playing a different genre. There’s little today that aims for that still-potent original survival horror mix of innovation, mystery, fear, and meaningful narrative.

Silent Hill: Townfall looks to respect that central tenet that glues the genre’s wider ideas together. It remembers that a compelling mystery guides a player through exploration, combat, and the fear that would otherwise root them to the ground. There is genuine mystery around Townfall’s story and themes, maintained even for journalists who have already played a few hours at trade shows . Assumptions can be made from the fact that protagonist Simon has a cannula in his veins, and that the game’s first monster’s body is bound by belts in a way that mirrors straitjacketing. But it seems that the story is more than just a straightforward look at horrific healthcare: there is clearly a knot of issues mouldering at the core of St. Amelia, with the small Scottish town abandoned and apparently in the grasp of a disdained corporation. Story seems to be at the forefront of the game, but importantly not frontloaded or plainly spelt out in journals, and so it’s pleasantly impossible to know how this will all unfurl.

The problem with survival horror’s wider resurgence is a repeat of what undermined the genre historically: mechanics and structure moving so far away from the core that they can no longer reasonably be called survival horror. People who have held the torch for it across so many years have held that love because it’s not driven by modern trends; that it prioritises atmosphere, themes, and deep cuts for its influences, like ‘70s Italian horror. Silent Hill: Townfall seems to realise that the genre is more than cherry-picking elements; more than taking some horrible creatures or sweat-inducing mechanics. Maybe this can encourage other developers to realise that people don’t fear the conventions of survival horror, and take the admirable, classic-creating risk of bringing true, distinctive, and - above all - ambiguous fear to the fore.

Ceridwen Millington is a journalist, gamer, and reader who is almost always ready to dive into horror.

articles.title: Harry Potter TV Series Casts Arthur Weasley, Moaning Myrtle and Colin Creevey
articles.summary: HBO's Harry Potter TV series has found its Arthur Weasley, Moaning Myrtle and Colin Creevey, with Rafe Spall cast as Ron's dad.
articles.body:
HBO's Harry Potter TV series has found its Arthur Weasley, Moaning Myrtle, and Colin Creevey, with Rafe Spall cast as Ron's dad.

Spall currently stars in Apple TV series Trying, though has also had roles in Life of Pi, Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom, Men in Black: International, and Black Mirror.

Portrayed by Mark Williams in the original Harry Potter movies, Arthur Weasley is the good-natured patriarch of the Weasley family, and a recurring character through the Harry Potter series from the second book onwards.

It is Arthur's love of Muggle objects that ensures Harry and Ron can get to Hogwarts in an enchanted Ford Anglia, and in later stories Arthur's position in the Ministry of Magic allows Harry to hear the inner workings of the wizarding world as Voldemort ascends to power.

Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone TV Show Character Images

Other roles announced today include ghostly schoolgirl Moaning Myrtle and the photography-obsessed Colin Creevey. Both have small roles throughout the series, though first pop up in Chamber of Secrets as victims of a mysterious creature slithering around Hogwarts castle. Here, the pair will be played by newcomers Molly Hewitt-Richards and Jasper Ambrose, respectively.

Earlier this month, HBO announced a trio of other key roles for its second season of its Harry Potter adaptation , which now has actors cast for Tom Riddle (AKA the young Lord Voldemort), Dobby the house-elf and a new face for Ginny Weasley. Game of Thrones star Kit Harington will play Gilderoy Lockhart , meanwhile, filling in for Tom Hoult who dropped out due to a recent filming delay.

This month also brought our best look yet at the series' upcoming first season, including a peek at Quidditch, Professor Snape and the Sorting Hat . That's due to begin airing at Christmas this year, with the now-filming second season expected to follow in late 2027 or 2028.

articles.title: Apex Legends VS Street Fighter Brings Chun-Li, Ryu, Akuma, and More to the Outlands
articles.summary: Street Fighter is coming to Apex Legends on September 22, bringing its high-kicking action to the first-person battle royale with special skins, a decked-out POI, a Wildcard Takeover, and more.
articles.body:
Street Fighter is coming to Apex Legends on September 22, bringing its high-kicking action to the first-person battle royale with special skins, a decked-out POI, a Wildcard Takeover, and more.

This collaboration hurricane-kicks its way into the Outlands on Tuesday, September 22 at 10am PT / 1pm ET. We’ve outlined everything you can expect from Apex Legends’ Street Fighter makeover below.

Players will have the chance to nab eight Iconic Skins in the Reward Shop that transform their Legends into characters from Capcom’s beloved fighting game franchise, as well as one Epic Skin for Lifeline as Li-Fen, Chun-Li’s protege in Street Fighter 6’s World Tour story mode. We’ve included a list of all these characters below, as well as comments about the skins from Apex Legends’ art director, Alisa Rastorgueva, from a closed session with the media:

● Sparrow as Ryu: “We’re really thinking about personality, playstyle, silhouette when matching our Apex Legends with their Street Fighter counterparts. Sparrow felt the closest to Ryu's grisly self in Street Fighter 6 specifically, and we really wanted to push the muscle definition for this skin.”

● Alter as Chun-Li: “We wanted to make sure Alter could do Chun-Li justice. We pushed the silhouettes of these models and bodies.”

● Mirage as Luke: “Luke is Street Fighter 6’s breakout character, so we really wanted to feature him. Mirage felt like an obvious match in terms of personality, since they never take themselves seriously.”

● Gibraltar as Akuma: “This was definitely a fun skin for Gibby. His size and silhouette gave us a good canvas to bring that to life.”

● Wattson as Cammy: “They really complement each other. How Wattson operates matches well with Cammy’s fighting style.”

● Caustic as Blanka: “Blanka is big, unpredictable, and terrifying. One detail we are really proud of here are Caustic’s canisters: As you can see here, they feature electric eels that we hope fans catch and appreciate.”

● Pathfinder as Dhalsim: "Figuring out how to put Dahlsim's design on a robot was definitely a challenge.”

Apex Legends x Street Fighter 6 Collaboration Images

Eight new Legendary Street Fighter 6-themed weapon skins are also available in the Reward Shop:

Other goodies include two new Skydive Emotes (one of them is a Tatsumaki), Holosprays, stickers (these include all characters in Street Fighter 6’s base roster), badges, trackers, and frames.

To really get players into the Street Fighter spirit, the devs at Respawn have lovingly prepared a new Hadouken Universal Melee cosmetic that includes a matching Deathbox. This allows players to literally throw out a Hadouken projectile in the middle of battle; just don’t fall prey to the Dark Hadou!

Olympus is getting a Street Fighter makeover; the entire area has been decked out in bright colors, graffiti, giant Blanka-chan balloons, and even silver statues of the eight characters featured as skins in this collaboration. Punch Trucks are scattered throughout the POI, which players can beat up using melee attacks to earn Fight Gauge tokens in traditional Street Fighter fashion.

That’s not all; Pathfinder’s Fight Night has been transformed into Luke’s Gym, featuring arcade cabinets, Street Fighter 6-branded punching bags, a weight rack, and of course, Luke’s signature blue and orange colors. There’s even a massive screen surrounding the entire area featuring Ryu and Chun-Li facing off, which will loom over the match in its entirety.

“Remixing Olympus for this takeover was all about immersing players in fighting game culture, world director Eduardo Agostini said. “Building off what we learned on maps like Night City E-District, we wanted Olympus to feel like a living Street Fighter stage. For the Street Fighter 6 collaboration especially, we kept thinking of how we could inject that high-energy arcade feel directly into the map. …We’re really excited for players to explore every corner of this map and feel the energy that the team poured into it.”

The Apex Legends x Street Fighter collab also features a Wildcard Takeover that transforms the first-person shooter into an all-out brawl. Rather than firing bullets at other players, you’ll use your Street Fighter skills to punch and kick your opponents. For this mode, the devs at Respawn cleaned up the game’s melee to let players perform fluid combos, which will fill your Fighter Gauge. Collecting tokens throughout the area will also fill your gauge, allowing you to enter Fighter Form, a third-person combat mode with new Tactical and Ultimate abilities, movement, and blocking capabilities.

Titled Apex KO, players will need to select one of four fighters before entering the match as either Ryu, Chun-Li, Dhalsim and Akuma. If you don’t make a choice, one will be selected for you. When you enter Fighter Form, your abilities will be replaced with skills that suit each Street Fighter character. Some of these are listed below:

Ryu: Shin Shoryuken, Dash, Hadouken. (You can lock onto targets to hit them with the hadouken but it won’t do exploding damage.)

(You can lock onto targets to hit them with the hadouken but it won’t do exploding damage.)

Chun-Li: Double-jump, Kikouken, Kikosho, and faster melee attack speed.

Dhalsim: Increased melee range, Teleportation, Yoga sunburst.

Akuma: Gohadouken, Shun Goku Satsu, Raging Demon, Demon Mode.

The final round is called the Showdown, where any downed or respawning players rejoin the fight to throw hands until one squad is left standing.

“At its core, Apex is built on competition,” Chris Ruvolo, senior technical game designer for Apex Legends, said in a statement. “Translating Street Fighter 6’s mechanics into a third-person Battle Royale experience was about finding those synergies in their shared competitive DNA. Balancing the four Fighter Gear kits was such a fun opportunity to give players highly expressive tools like Hadokens, wall-runs and Yoga Teleports without compromising Apex’s core gameplay and competitive integrity. The final Showdown round distills that drive into a high-stakes brawl where clutch execution decides who survives.”

articles.title: Apex Legends Art Director Says Street Fighter 6 Pushed Devs to Give Characters the 'Thickest Thighs' They've Ever Had
articles.summary: Apex Legends art director Alisa Rastorgueva revealed that the developers pushed the limits of the game’s character models so far for its collaboration with Street Fighter 6 that its heroes became “thicker” than ever.
articles.body:
Apex Legends art director Alisa Rastorgueva says developers pushed the limits of the game’s character models so far for its collaboration with Street Fighter 6 that its heroes became “thicker” than ever.

Street Fighter 6 is coming to Apex Legends with special character skins, a decked-out POI, an ambitious Wildcard Takover, weapon skins, and more on September 22.

To celebrate, a handful of Legends are getting the Street Fighter treatment, transforming them into characters from Capcom’s beloved fighting game franchise: Sparrow is Ryu; Alter is Chun-Li; Mirage is Luke; Caustic is Blanka; Wattson is Cammy; Gibraltar is Akuma; Bangalore is Elena; and Pathfinder is Dhalsim.

Apex Legends x Street Fighter 6 Collaboration Images

Each fighter in this delightful selection of characters boasts a striking silhouette with the muscles to match (they are martial artists, after all) — and that was something that challenged the art team when it came to literally breaking the mold of their Legends to make them look like their Street Fighter counterparts.

In a closed session with the media, Apex Legends art director Alisa Rastorgueva revealed that these Street Fighter skins were so muscular that the Legends now have the thickest thighs they’ve ever made for the game.

“There’s always a new challenge with every collab that we do, and it’s always different,” she told us. “With Gundam, it was trying to fit our Legends into these big mechs. For Street Fighter, a big challenge was trying to find a balance between pushing the body types, especially the muscle definition. All of us know that Street Fighter characters are muscular and their proportions are pushed a lot. We tried to do that, as well. Our legends have some of the thickest thighs we’ve ever done. To take an IP with that much history behind it and put it into Apex Legends — our game is semi-realistic, it definitely has a different visual style than Street Fighter has in a lot of their games, and for us, that was one of our biggest challenges. But it was a fun one.”

She also delved into the selection process for choosing these specific Street Fighter characters, explaining that there were many fighters the team considered bringing into the game, but only a few made sense to pair with their Legends.

“It’s just what worked best for this collaboration,” she said. “All of the pairings we do are a collaborative effort between our departments and the IP holder. We definitely wanted to have the Street Fighter characters represented well and be recognizable within the game, and this worked best with Alter and Sparrow. You can see characters like Chun-Li and Ryu very clearly when it’s designed on them versus other Legends. We do test characters for all the pairings, and we ended up working with [Sparrow and Alter] once again.”

Senior technical game designer Chris Ruvolo added that it wasn’t just a matter of physicality, but of gameplay, as well; putting a grappler like Zangief in a first-person shooter like Apex Legends wouldn’t really make sense for the type of game it is, despite how cool it’d be.

“There were a lot that we wanted to add that we couldn't,” he admitted. “We really wanted to highlight characters from Street Fighter 6 specifically. Unfortunately, I wish we could do the full roster, but we weren’t able to. We highlighted some of the characters that worked best for us and our IP partner.

“Me and my manager played a lot of Street Fighter 6,” he continued. “We got all the fighter passes and played around with them to see what would work best for Apex. It was kinda tough figuring out what characters to bring in, since Apex is primarily a shooter. You can't have a fighter who focuses on grapples like Zangief. We had to go with characters who were projectile-based or had area of effect attacks; those were at the top of our list. The creative process was, ‘What are some characters that players are gonna recognize? Which will fit well within Apex’s gameplay?’”

You can brawl it out in the new Wildcard Takeover, punch destructible cars, and even pull off a Hadouken when Street Fighter hurricane-kicks its way into Apex Legends on September 22.

articles.title: Metroid Ravenous Preorders Are Already $10 Off at Amazon and Walmart
articles.summary: Save $10 on physical copies of Metroid Ravenous for Nintendo Switch 2 at Walmart, plus learn how a promo code could potentially drop the price even further to $49.88.
articles.body:
Physical copies of Metroid Ravenous for Nintendo Switch 2 are now $10 off at Walmart, following the discounts provided to other recent Nintendo preorders such as The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake. That brings the game down to $59.88, over $10 off the original MSRP of $69.99.

Preorders for Metroid Ravenous went live not long after its standout trailer during the recent Nintendo Direct . There's been plenty of excitement since, and we've even seen preorders for the Metroid Ravenous Special Edition completely sell out in minutes across most retailers since the reveal.

But $10 off the standard edition of the game isn't a bad consolation prize if you were unable to secure a preorder for the special edition.

Yet, what's the deal with the immediate $10 discount at Walmart? Well, it's actually fairly simple. As is Nintendo's custom for this console generation , the MSRP for the game is $59.99 for digital copies and $69.99 for physical copies.

We've seen the same thing with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, Star Fox , Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave , and Switch Sports Resort , among others. It's a pretty easy way to save $10 if you're planning to buy a physical copy anyway.

Amazon has always price matched the deal every single time, so you can also preorder there as well.

The only thing to bear in mind is that these discounts are generally tied to the preorder period. Once Metroid Ravenous actually releases, I wouldn't expect this $59.88 price to stick around.

At least there's no compromise with the physical release itself, either. Metroid Ravenous comes with the full game on the cartridge, so there's no game key card nonsense to deal with here.

More Metroid Games Are on Sale Right Now

Looking to play some more Metroid before Ravenous comes out next year? I've got you covered there as well.

As part of Nintendo's Customer Appreciation Sale , Metroid Dread is currently $41.99, down from its usual $59.99 . That's not quite the lowest price we've seen the Switch classic hit ($39), but an $18 saving is still pretty decent for such an incredible game.

But, there are a couple of other Metroid games to check out in the sale as well. That includes Metroid Prime Remastered for $27.97 , and Metroid Prime 4: Beyond for $41.99 .

Metroid Ravenous is set to launch exclusively for Nintendo Switch 2 on January 28, 2027.

A follow-up to Metroid Dread, it’s a new 2D side-scrolling adventure for Samus, the space-faring bounty hunter.

In the trailer, Samus says, “I was attacked by unknown assailants and sustained grave injuries. I don't know where I am, getting back to the surface won't be easy."

"My chances of getting off this moon are slim at best. Still... I will survive. And I will make it home. Even if I have to feed on my enemies to do so. It's eat or be eaten."

This very much looks like Metroid Dread 2, with Samus look just as brutal and animalistic as she was at the end of the last game. I'm fully on board for this.

Metroid Ravenous amiibo Preorders Are Back in Stock

Chozo Statue amiibo - Metroid Ravenous Series

Releasing alongside the game are two additional amiibos: Samus and Chozo Statue.

They have been hard to come by, but Best Buy has recently kicked off a fresh wave of preorders. It's your best place to secure the two new amiibo right now.

articles.title: The Golden Axe Animated Series Brings Star Trek: Lower Decks Energy to Its Adaptation of the Game Series
articles.summary: Golden Axe Animated Series review: Mike McMahan brings Lower Decks energy to this animated adaptation of the game series.
articles.body:
Golden Axe debuts September 16 on Paramount+.

It’s understandable to feel somewhat cynical and pre-exhausted about Golden Axe going into it, simply because the entire approach of a snarky, self-aware animated series is, generally speaking, very well worn territory at this point and can feel like something of a safety net rather than trying for a more straightforward and earnest approach. Then there’s also the fact that joke-driven fantasy stories in particular are also quite familiar terrain both in and out of animation, encompassing everything from The Princess Bride to Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves.

Having seen the entire first season, I can say that Golden Axe is certainly doing what you’d expect, as it takes the characters and concepts from the 1989 SEGA game and its sequels and remixes them into a decidedly wacky, high energy cartoon. But after some initial bumps in the road, the series gradually grew on me through its ten episodes thanks to some solid laughs, great voice acting, and its overall good nature.

Obviously adapting any familiar IP is tricky territory, as fans can be just a tiny bit possessive and sensitive about how a beloved pre-existing universe is handled — just ask Zach Cregger — but Golden Axe feels like a safer title than some for going this route. Its heyday was in the arcade era, its most recent installment was a poorly received 2008 game , and it never had the deepest or most complex mythology. Of course, you’ll still find many many angry comments below Golden Axe’s trailer saying that they’re upset that this is a comedic take on the serious property they remember. I get it, but also… it’s Golden Axe, guys! It’s a genuinely fun game, but as someone who’s old enough to have fond memories of playing the original in arcades, it’s also not a title we need to be precious about, especially given that this show never feels spiteful about its source material.

The game’s original heroic trio of Ax Battler, Tyris Flare, and Gilius Thunderhead all play large roles here, but the story kicks off with Gilius having a spat with the others that leads to him splitting off from them on a parallel quest through the land of Yuria alongside an overeager protogree named Hampton Squib, who’s the main new addition to the canon in this series. Meanwhile, Ax and Tyris replace Gilius with Chronos, a character culled from Golden Axe III , while all the characters simultaneously hope to take down the villainous Death Adder, who has control of the powerful weapon known as the Golden Axe.

If there’s a lead character in this ensemble, it’s definitely Gilius the battle dwarf, voiced here by the always excellent Matthew Rhys, currently riding high on much deserved adoration for Widow’s Bay. Rhys is incredibly fun playing the crusty and stubborn Gilius, going big when the scene calls for it in all the right ways. If you’ve enjoyed hearing him yell out in terror on Widow’s Bay, you’ll also enjoy some of Rhys’ reactions here, including an especially prolonged scream at one point.

Voicing Hampton, Danny Pudi makes for a perfect partner for Rhys, bringing just the right kind of youthful, optimistic energy the character calls for (it doesn’t matter that Pudi’s pushing 50 in real life; this is a cartoon!). And Liam McIntyre, Lisa Gilroy, and Carl Tart all know exactly the kind of humorously self-confident vibes with which to imbue their characters, voicing Ax, Tyris, and Chronos respectively.

Still, with the show keeping our heroes in two distinct groups for so much of the season, there’s stronger material for the Gilius and Hampton portions overall, with the dimwitted Ax and the arrogant Tyris sometimes providing too similar of a feel with their single-minded, overconfident approach. Chronos the cat man — or panther man if you ask him — at least provides a different, more offbeat energy.

The tone and sense of humor of Golden Axe evokes the likes of Rick and Morty and Star Trek: Lower Decks, and also replicates the strengths and weaknesses of those series and others like them. This isn’t a shock, given that Golden Axe has writers who worked on Rick and Morty, and that one of the two creators — Mike McMahan, teamed here with Joe Chandler — was in fact the creator of Lower Decks as well.

Like those series, Golden Axe is rapid fire with its jokes, with mixed results. There are some duds to be sure, and some gags are way too telegraphed or obvious, but there are also many really strong and even outright hysterical moments as well as we watch these guys and their enemies hack and slash their way across the land, mega-gore included. One particularly strong ongoing element is how the series uses the game’s skeleton warriors, who get to represent all sorts of different mundane personality types as we see them make small talk, bully one another, or complain when they can’t hear their boss’ big speech.

Shades of Lower Decks and Rick and Morty, Golden Axe can be a lot at times, feeling overly frenetic and sometimes outright abrasive with its in-your-face approach. But after the early episodes lean dangerously far in this direction, the pacing improves as the season continues, and the characters become better defined and more likable, including the addition of a notably upbeat skeleton voiced by the always welcome presence of Stephanie Beatriz.

The show rarely breaks the fourth wall outright — though the funny offscreen narrator, voiced by SungWon Cho, certainly pushes things further — but continually takes a winking approach to both video game tropes in general and to elements of Golden Axe specifically. Yes, the wonderfully ridiculous name Ax Battler, and the fact that the dude uses a sword and not an axe, is addressed in a scene that is both amusing yet also certainly low-hanging fruit.

I particularly loved how the show incorporates the magic potions from the game, and the bizarre manner in which you’d replenish those potions by literally kicking small little creatures known as Thieves. The show’s exploration of what exactly the deal is with one of these Thieves, his home life included, is one of the season’s highlights. Also a standout is the fifth episode of the season, which comes up with a plot device to directly recreate the game’s imagery in an entertaining manner.

The self-parody and winking approach feels like it’s done with affection in Golden Axe. As with Lower Decks, it’s comedically deconstructing the familiar aspects of the IP with which it’s working, but from the perspective of someone who definitely understands and knows the original well. It doesn’t come across as either mockery or self-loathing, because yes, the beast from the games known as Chicken Leg is in this show, and yes, he’s very silly but he’s also very lovable.

articles.title: Rockstar Games Begins Teasing GTA 6's Soundtrack With Travis Scott, Future, Morgan Wallen, and More
articles.summary: Rockstar Games has begun teasing the soundtrack for Grand Theft Auto 6 with new artwork from Future, Travis Scott, and other artists.
articles.body:
Rockstar Games has begun teasing the soundtrack for Grand Theft Auto 6 with new artwork from Future, Travis Scott, and other artists.

Travis Scott, Future, and Morgan Wallen have all posted zoomed-in pictures of a larger piece of artwork from Grand Theft Auto 6. Scott's image featured a woman's heeled feet and was paired with a caption mentioning Rockstar, while Wallen's was a caption-less image of a pool ladder in Rockstar's art style. Many assumed that these were all teasing GTA 6 in some capacity, and that was confirmed once Future uploaded a picture of a sports car repping a Leonida license plate. Metro Boomin and Yung Lean also posted the same image as Future on their respective profiles. Argentine hip hop duo CA7RIEL & Paco Amoroso also posted their own image, which featured a yacht.

Presumably, there will be more of these posts from other artists throughout the day, so we will continue to keep this article updated as more images roll in.

It's likely that all of these singers will have music in the game, but it's unclear if they have larger roles as characters in the game or radio hosts. Dr. Dre was prominently featured as a character in GTA Online, Phil Colins was a character in Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories, and a number of comedians like Ricky Gervais have appeared in the flesh in games like GTA 4, so there's precedent for them to appear as actual characters. Actor Stephen Root also confirmed his long speculated role as Brian Heder in GTA 6 earlier this week, though seemingly through a slip-up rather than a planned reveal.

This appears to be just one part of Rockstar Games' massive marketing push for GTA 6, which properly kicked off this summer with pre-orders and an extensive gameplay reveal that debuted on Netflix. Rockstar is expected to keep its foot on the gas until launch, which is almost exactly two months away now.

articles.title: Fable Developer Explains Why Xbox 'Protected' the Project Over Its Long Development Cycle, Amid Layoffs and Studio Closures Elsewhere
articles.summary: Fable maker Playground Games has detailed how its upcoming RPG survived a decade in development, amid layoffs and studio closures across the rest of Xbox.
articles.body:
Fable maker Playground Games has detailed how its upcoming RPG survived a decade in development, amid layoffs and studio closures across the rest of Xbox.

Early work on building Fable's team began in 2017, just a year after Microsoft shut down classic Fable maker Lionhead Studios. 10 years on, Playground Games' Fable will finally launch after a mammoth development, into a very different gaming landscape.

When work on Fable began, Xbox was still to acquire We Happy Few maker Compulsion Games, Psychonauts studio Double Fine, State of Decay developer Undead Labs, or Hellblade team Ninja Theory — all companies it subsequently cast adrift this summer. Xbox was yet to set up The Initiative, the team it pumped millions into for the purposes of making Perfect Dark, then closed after 7 years with nothing to show for it. There was no sign Xbox would splash out $7.5 billion on Bethesda (including id, MachineGames, and the now-divested Tango Gameworks). And there was certainly no inkling it would drop $68.7 billion on Activision Blizzard.

Likewise, there was no telling that Microsoft's many acquisitions would be followed by successive waves of layoffs. 1,900 jobs were slashed in January 2024, many from the newly-acquired Activision Blizzard, while at least 650 staff were let go later that year, and Redfall maker Arkane Austin was closed. Last year, meanwhile, 9,000 staff departed Microsoft as the company pivoted towards AI spending, wiping out The Initiative and scores of workers from both Forza Motorsport team Turn 10 and veteran British outfit Rare, which saw its meandering work on Everwild ended after more than a decade.

And there were this year's layoffs, the first to come from new Xbox boss Asha Sharma. These will ultimately end up hitting 3,200 workers, with significant doubt now placed on the future of Marvel's Blade maker Arkane Lyon.

So, how did Fable survive all of that? Speaking to The Guardian , director Ralph Fulton explained that the Fable franchise simply remained "vital" to Xbox.

"I genuinely think Fable is an important game," Fulton said. "What has protected us over a long development cycle is that so many people within Xbox view Fable as vital to the DNA of the platform.

"I would go a step further and say it's important to video games as a whole," he continued. "It offers a combination of elements that simply doesn't exist anywhere else."

Video games do not typically get the luxury of having decade-long development cycles, and it does feel like Fable is one of Xbox's few core brands that remain central to the platform, alongside Halo, Forza and Gears of War. Compared to these, it's perhaps not a surprise to see Xbox push on with the game's lengthy road to release, even as it ditched untested ideas like Everwild (which seemed some way from release still, even after a decade in the oven). And then there's the fact that, while one team within Playground was busy building Fable, another was just as busy pumping out its hugely-successful and well-regarded Forza Horizon games, which will certainly have helped pay the bills.

Whatever the case, we're very happy Fable is now nearing the end of its journey — and looking forward to playing it when it finally arrives on February 23, 2027.

Tom Phillips is IGN's News Editor. You can reach Tom at tom_phillips@ign.com or find him on Bluesky @tomphillipseg.bsky.social

articles.title: How The Oregon Trail became a generational icon
articles.summary: The story of Oregon Trail, one of the most iconic edutainment computer games of all time, on Version History.
articles.body: Whether you played it in the back of your classroom or on your computer at home, if you were a kid in the last 30 years you almost certainly grew up playing The Oregon Trail. On the season 5 premiere of Version History, our fearless wagon leader David Pierce is joined by gaming journalist Chris Grant and Philip Bouchard, the designer and team leader of the game’s most iconic version. They talk about the academic origins of The Oregon Trail, the game’s complicated legacy, and whether anyone ever really died of dysentery. This is the first episode of the fifth season of Version History, and this time we’re going back to school. In the weeks to come, we’re taking on the iconic TI-84 graphing calculator, One Laptop Per Child, Chromebook, LeapPad, and the overhead projector. Plus, this Friday, we’ll livestream a playthrough of The Oregon Trail from The Verge’s YouTube channel. Find out which Verge staffers make it to the end, and which ones fall along the way. Each pack even guarantees a foil. If you haven’t checked it out yet, MTG: Lorwyn Eclipsed is a really nice set full of awesome fantasy creatures.

The GameSir Cyclone 2 Wireless Pro Controller is only $40.10 on AliExpress through the official GameSir store. Just enter the code “FSUS04” at checkout for extra savings, plus shipping is included. While the Switch 2 Pro Controller is one of the best controllers for Nintendo’s latest console, it’s pricey. articles.title: Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2's Nintendo Switch 2 Version Delayed to Early 2027
articles.summary: Cold Iron Studios, developer of the recently released four-player co-op PvE sequel Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2, has announced that the Nintendo Switch 2 version has been pushed back to early 2027. It was originally planned to ship this month.
articles.body:
Cold Iron Studios, developer of the recently released four-player co-op PvE sequel Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2, has announced that the Nintendo Switch 2 version has been pushed back to early 2027. It was originally planned to ship this month.

"After careful consideration, we now plan to release it natively on Switch 2 in early 2027," the studio said in a statement. "This extra time will help the team deliver the best possible version for the hardware. Thank you for your patience and understanding. In the meantime, the team at Cold Iron remains aggressively focused on tuning Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 to be the best possible experience for every player."

Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 is the second major third-party game today that's pushed back its planned Nintendo Switch 2 version. IO Interactive also announced that 007: First Light won't see the light of day on Nintendo's newest hardware until early next year.

IGN gave the PC, Xbox, and PlayStation version of Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 a 7 out of 10 , saying in part, "Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 isn’t going to make you leave a co-op shooter you already love at the altar, but it is a good time with friends."

articles.title: Xbox Game Pass September 2026 Wave 2 Lineup Announced
articles.summary: Microsoft has announced the Xbox Game Pass September 2027 Wave 2 lineup, and it includes Dune Awakening, plus Minecraft Dungeons 2 and Gears of War: E-Day for Ultimate and PC subscribers.
articles.body:
Microsoft has announced the Xbox Game Pass September 2027 Wave 2 lineup, and it includes Dune Awakening, plus Minecraft Dungeons 2 and Gears of War: E-Day for Ultimate and PC subscribers.

Sandy survival RPG Dune: Awakening is amongst this month's biggest additions, and lands for Game Pass Premium, PC and Ultimate subscribers on September 22. PC and Ultimate subscribers will meanwhile get day-one access to Minecraft Dungeons 2 and Gears of War: E-Day on September 29 and October 6, respectively.

Also worth a look this month are comicbook beat 'em up Marvel Cosmic Invasion, sci-fi puzzler Planet of Lana 2, Call of Duty: Black Ops 6 and Ninja Gaiden 4, all of which join Xbox Game Pass Premium. If you've yet to try it already, Premium subscribers also get to play Keeper, just as the game also pops up on PlayStation 5.

Other titles on offer include bike-racing party game Ultimate Sheep Raccoon, sci-fi horror Routine, action RPG roguelike Kernel Hearts, dark fairytale Metroidvania Well Dweller and 2.5D roguelite beat 'em up Mad King Redemption. Anything tickle your fancy?

RuneScape: Dragonwilds (Cloud, Xbox Series X/S, and PC) – September 15, Game Pass Ultimate, Game Pass Premium, PC Game Pass

Marvel Cosmic Invasion (Cloud, Xbox Series X/S, Handheld, and PC) – September 16, now with Game Pass Premium; joining Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass

Dune: Awakening (Cloud, Xbox Series X/S, Handheld, and PC) – September 22, Game Pass Ultimate, Game Pass Premium, PC Game Pass

Well Dweller (Cloud, Console, Handheld, and PC) – September 22, Game Pass Ultimate, PC Game Pass

Gears of War: E-Day (Xbox Series X/S, Handheld, PC, and Cloud) – October 6, Game Pass Ultimate, PC Game Pass

As always, whenever Microsoft giveth, it also taketh away. A number of games leave Game Pass this month, including the rather British-feeling Fallout-like, Atomfall. Be sure to play that before it departs, as well as everything else listed below:
